perspective:
I am Harold Padilla, a project manager. I know Arthur Begum as a friend/advisor and a police officer. I have a project team whose progress and motivation concern me.

- I felt frustrated and anxious because my project team seemed unmotivated, and it was affecting our progress. I arranged to meet Arthur at a coffee shop.
- I told Arthur I was at my wit’s end because the team seemed unmotivated. Arthur asked if I had tried understanding what drives each team member individually. I admitted I hadn’t, since I’d been focused on project goals and deadlines. Arthur advised one-on-one conversations to see what was going on and to help people feel valued and understood. I said I would try it and felt more hopeful.
- I told my team we would have quick one-on-one chats to understand what motivates each of them, believing it would help us work better together. Team Member 1 said that could be helpful. Team Member 2 said they were open to it. I said I would schedule time with each of them and wanted us to make the project a success together.
- After implementing Arthur’s advice, I noticed the team still was not responding well. I felt disappointed and worried about the project’s future. I told Arthur I had tried his suggestions but the team still wasn’t responding. Arthur said there might be deeper issues, such as personal conflicts, lack of trust, or external stressors, and that I might need to dig deeper. I said I would set up another round of meetings to get to the bottom of it.
- In one-on-one meetings, I asked team members to share concerns or problems. Team Member 1 told me there was tension between a few people that was affecting work. Team Member 2 told me they felt overwhelmed by the workload and stressed, making it hard to stay motivated. I thanked them, said I would look into resolving conflicts, and said I would see about redistributing tasks to ease pressure; their well-being mattered to me.
- Feeling optimistic and empowered, I told the team we would have regular feedback sessions and team-building activities to create a more supportive environment. Team Member 1 said that sounded great and would help us work better together. Team Member 2 agreed and said it was good that their concerns were being addressed. I said I was glad and urged us to work together to make the project a success, saying their input and well-being were crucial.
